served.stem: Why is HF's BP higher than HCl's, even though HCl is heavier?
served.bankWhy: F can H-bond (NOF rule). Cl cannot. H-bond strength > extra LDF gain.

answer.line: H on F lets HF molecules hydrogen bond. That pull is far stronger than the extra London force HCl gets from its extra electrons.

steps: Name the strongest force in each liquid first. HF has H bonded to F, so it hydrogen bonds; HCl has only dipole-dipole and London forces.
Weigh the trade. HCl is heavier, so its London forces are bigger, but a hydrogen bond outweighs that gain.
More pull between molecules means more heat to separate them: HF boils near 20 degrees C, HCl near -85.

choices.note: Metallic bonding holds metals together with a shared sea of electrons. HF and HCl are small molecules.
London forces grow with electron count, so HCl has the stronger ones. HF wins on hydrogen bonding instead.
Hydrogen bonds outweigh HCl's extra London force.
Pure HCl is a polar covalent molecule. It splits into ions only when dissolved in water.
Density does not set a boiling point. How hard the molecules pull on each other does.
